title: Gideon and the Cellar
premise: Ulyana Galloway, an urban explorer who has spent seven years mapping the unmapped tunnels beneath the dying village of Kessel's Hollow, has always explained away the noises—settling pipes, wind, her own mind. But when the church bell rings at midnight despite having been melted down in 1911, she realizes the tunnels are counting something, or someone, down. The last resident of the village, elderly Tomas Vey, is about to sign papers that will hand the land to a development company whose founders' names match those carved into the cellar walls in 1911. Ulyana discovers the bell rings each time a name on an old parish ledger is 'collected,' and that staying invisible—her lifelong strategy for survival as a trans woman estranged from the village that raised her—was never really an option: the count includes her family name. To save Tomas and her own kin, she must lead them out ahead of the final toll, confronting the thing in the cellar that feeds on debts unpaid and identities denied. In the end, Ulyana signs nothing, gives the cellar what it actually wants—the truth spoken aloud—and the bell cracks mid-toll, freeing the village but leaving her forever changed, half-heard even in silence.
about_author: Freya Nystrom is the pen name of a former surveyor who spent a decade documenting abandoned infrastructure across northern Europe before turning to horror fiction. They write stories about places that remember what people would rather forget.

chapters.title: The Map That Grows
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She descends into the Kessel's Hollow tunnels to add new passages to her seven-year map and finds a corridor that wasn't there last month, its walls scored with tally marks. The emotional beat is quiet unease—the thrill of discovery curdling into the sense of being expected.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, with flashbacks. She catalogs every noise she's rationalized over seven years—dripping water, settling stone—and admits some explanations no longer hold. Her journal entries reveal her deeper secret: she grew up here, before leaving as Daniel Galloway. The beat is dread layered over grief.

chapters.title: A Bell That Should Not Ring
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. At midnight the church bell tolls once; Ulyana confirms the bell was melted down in 1911, its metal sold to fund the war effort. The village's few remaining residents pretend not to have heard it. The beat is the collapse of her rational worldview.

chapters.title: Tomas Vey Signs Nothing Yet
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The last permanent resident reviews the development company's purchase papers, disturbed that the firm's letterhead bears names he remembers from gravestones. He almost burns the documents, then doesn't. The beat is stubborn, frightened dignity.

chapters.title: The Parish Ledger
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. In the sealed vestry she finds the 1911 parish ledger: a list of names, most struck through in dried brown ink, including Galloway. Beside it, a fresh column has begun filling in pencil. The beat is cold recognition—her family name is already written.

chapters.title: What the Cellar Keeps
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She traces the tunnel to a cellar beneath the ruined church where the tally marks end at a door bound in bell-metal. Something behind it breathes in rhythm with her own pulse. The beat is terror tempered by terrible familiarity.

chapters.title: The Company of Old Names
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, Ulyana and Tomas. Ulyana researches the development firm, Hallow & Vey Estates, and finds its founding partners died in 1911—all of them, same week. Tomas receives a second set of papers, more insistent. The beat is paranoia becoming pattern.

chapters.title: Second Toll
chapters.summary: Multiple brief POVs across the village. The bell rings twice; two residents who had planned to stay through winter abruptly pack their cars and leave, eyes empty. The ledger's pencil column gains two strokes. The beat is communal denial fracturing.

chapters.title: Daniel in the Dark
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, deep flashback. Seven years ago she fled Kessel's Hollow after coming out, and something in the tunnels called her by her old name all the way to the county line. She understands now why she kept returning. The beat is painful self-reckoning.

chapters.title: The Count Explained
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. He tells Ulyana what his grandmother whispered: the cellar collects on the village's oldest debt—a life promised in 1911 and never delivered—and it counts down by bell until the debt is paid or the village empties. The beat is grim inheritance.

chapters.title: Third Toll
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The third ring comes early, off-schedule, and this time it sounds like her childhood nickname. The door in the cellar has a hairline crack. She photographs everything and the photos develop wrong—each one showing the cellar door open. The beat is escalating violation.

chapters.title: Papers on the Table
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The company's representative arrives in person: a courteous woman whose face Ulyana recognizes from a 1911 photograph. Tomas stalls the signing, claiming his solicitor must review the deed. The beat is a duel of patience between the living and the patient dead.

chapters.title: Family
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She calls her estranged sister Marta, who still owns their mother's cottage in the village, and begs her to leave. Marta refuses—she has signed nothing, she owes nothing—but agrees to come see. The beat is fragile reconciliation over old wounds.

chapters.title: Fourth Toll
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Arriving at night, Marta hears the fourth ring and feels it in her teeth, in her bones, in the name she was called as a girl. She finds Ulyana's maps and finally believes her. The beat is belief arriving too late to be comfortable.

chapters.title: The Debt of 1911
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. In the vestry records they reconstruct the truth: in 1911 the village sold its bell and, secretly, promised one soul from the Galloway line to whatever the founders had woken in the cellar. The promise was never kept because Daniel's grandfather ran. The beat is horrified clarity.

chapters.title: Fifth Toll
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Five rings; the cellar door stands open and the tunnels begin rearranging themselves around the house, herding. Ulyana realizes the count isn't of days—it's of names, and hers is next after Tomas refuses to sign. The beat is cornered-animal resolve.

chapters.title: Evacuation
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Ulyana and Marta move the remaining residents out under cover of a gas-leak story, but Tomas won't go—he'll sign rather than let the thing follow them beyond the parish bounds. The beat is sacrifice offered and refused.

chapters.title: Sixth Toll
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Alone with the papers and the pen, Tomas hears six rings and understands the seventh will be the last whether he signs or not. He writes instead a confession of the 1911 promise, naming the debt honestly. The beat is courage found in an old man's honesty.

chapters.title: The Seventh Ring
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, climax. As the seventh toll begins, Ulyana descends into the open cellar and speaks the truth aloud—that the village lied, that she is a Galloway, that she chooses her own name and pays no one else's debts. The bell-metal door shudders. The beat is defiant self-assertion against a hungry old power.

chapters.title: Cracked
chapters.summary: Climax continued, ensemble POV. The bell rings itself apart mid-stroke; the tally marks run backward; the woman from 1911 unravels into dust and old resentment. The cellar exhales seven years of held breath. The beat is cathartic release through truth rather than violence.

chapters.title: After the Count
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The village is empty but not damned; Tomas burns the unsigned papers and leaves with Marta driving. Ulyana stays one last night and sleeps without hearing anything at all. The beat is exhausted peace.

chapters.title: Ulyana Galloway, Surveyor
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, resolution. Months later she publishes her map of the tunnels under her own full name, first time signing it publicly. On the final page, a single unexplained mark: a cracked bell, drawn in her own hand though she never drew it. The beat is identity claimed, haunting accepted.
